# Results — Study 902 (Multi-Factor Composite)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **single
factors take turns working, so an equal-weight blend of the five iShares single-factor ETFs
(VLUE value, QUAL quality, MTUM momentum, USMV min-vol, SIZE size), rebalanced monthly, beats
SPY on the excess-of-cash Sharpe with lower factor-timing risk, net of rebalancing costs** —
audited on monthly total returns over the window common to all five sleeves. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. Frozen
as-of 2026-06-30 (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).
Fingerprint `8b05ab0c64b8`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily auto-adjusted closes (**total-return**, net of each fund's fee) — VLUE, QUAL, MTUM, USMV, SIZE + SPY benchmark + BIL (SPDR 1-3-month T-bill ETF) as the tradable cash leg |
| Blend window | **2013-08-31 → 2026-06-30** (**155** complete months, common to all five sleeves; QUAL is the youngest, inception 2013-07) |
| Cash / risk-free | **BIL** total return — the excess-of-cash leg subtracts BIL from every series (excess-vs-excess race) |
| Composite | **equal-weight (1/5)**, rebalanced back to equal weight at each month-end; the incremental cost is the drift-rebalance turnover only (the one-time initial buy is common to any buy-and-hold benchmark) |
| Execution / costs | one-way **2 bps** per unit of rebalancing turnover (realistic large-ETF spread); long-only, **no shorts, no borrow**; SPY is buy-and-hold |

> **Selection / survivorship (named on the Signal axis).** These five are the flagship
> **surviving** iShares single-factor ETFs of the 2010s smart-beta launch wave (dozens of
> competitor factor ETFs closed). A blend of the five biggest survivors flatters the *average*
> multi-factor-ETF experience; it is the right panel only for the question asked — "did a blend
> of the flagship products beat the market?". The 155-month window is a single, largely
> large-cap-growth-led regime; the two-era cut is the honest robustness check within it.

## The composite sleeve (equal-weight, monthly rebalanced)

| leg | CAGR | vol | excess-Sharpe | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| composite **gross** | 13.33% | 14.1% | **0.841** | −23.7% |
| composite **net** (2 bps) | 13.32% | 14.1% | **0.841** | −23.7% |
| **SPY** | 14.14% | 14.5% | **0.874** | −23.9% |

Mean rebalancing turnover **1.17% of NAV/mo** → cost **0.02 bps/mo (~0.3 bps/yr)**. The five
factor ETFs are highly co-moving, so drift is small and the sleeve is nearly costless to run —
**gross and net are identical to two decimals**. This is decisive for the stamp: whatever the
sleeve is or isn't, **it is not a cost story**.

## Axis 1 — the excess-of-cash Sharpe race (both legs minus BIL)

| basis | comp exSharpe | SPY exSharpe | advantage | active (bps/mo) | active NW *t* | win-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| gross | 0.841 | 0.874 | **−0.033** | −6.4 | **−0.73** | — |
| net (2 bps) | 0.841 | 0.874 | **−0.033** | −6.5 | **−0.73** | 51% |

The composite lands **just short of the market** on risk-adjusted return: the Sharpe advantage
is **−0.033** (on the wrong side of zero), the active return **−6.5 bps/mo** at NW *t* =
**−0.73** — statistically indistinguishable from zero, and negative. The blend's vol (14.1%)
is a touch below SPY's (14.5%), but not enough to turn the Sharpe race.

## Axis 1b — bootstrap CI on the advantage (paired moving-block, net)

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| Sharpe advantage (comp − SPY) | **−0.033** |
| 95% CI (paired block bootstrap) | **[−0.205, +0.077]** — straddles zero |
| P(advantage < 0) | **0.804** |
| composite excess Sharpe (quantlab CBB) | 0.841, 95% CI [0.389, 1.373] |

The advantage CI comfortably contains zero; four draws in five put the sleeve *behind* SPY.
On 155 months the single-series Sharpe CI is itself wide (0.39–1.37) — there is no power here
to certify a market-beating edge that, at the point estimate, isn't even positive.

## Axis 2 — two-era robustness (the advantage is not stable)

| era | window | months | Sharpe adv | active (bps/mo) | active NW *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| early | 2013-08 → 2019-12 | 77 | **+0.078** | −0.1 | −0.02 |
| late | 2020-01 → 2026-06 | 78 | **−0.085** | −12.7 | −0.77 |

The advantage **flips sign across the halves** — marginally ahead pre-2020, further behind in
the 2020-26 mega-cap-growth tape. Not era-robust; the Real bar (clear of zero *and* stable
across sub-eras) is missed on both counts.

## Axis 3 — the diversification pitch (this half IS real)

| quantity | composite | benchmark | reading |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| annualised vol | **14.1%** | mean single sleeve **15.2%** (min 11.6%, SPY 14.5%) | blend cuts *level* risk below the average sleeve |
| excess Sharpe | **0.841** | mean single **0.786** (best single 0.928, SPY 0.874) | blend beats the *average* sleeve, trails the *best* and SPY |
| avg cross-sleeve annual dispersion | — | **7.0 pp/yr** | how far apart the five factors land each year (the timing risk of picking one)… |
| blend year-to-year sd | **11.9 pp** | — | …which the blend smooths |

Per single-factor sleeve, excess Sharpe on the common window: **MTUM 0.928**, QUAL 0.841,
USMV 0.780, VLUE 0.699, SIZE 0.681. The blend (0.841) lands where diversification predicts —
**above the average single sleeve, below the best** — and carries less vol and less
factor-timing dispersion than any single pick. That is a genuine, mechanical benefit; it is
diversification of *factor* risk, not of *market* risk, so it does not translate into beating
SPY.

## Robustness — inverse-vol weighting

Risk-weighting the sleeve by inverse trailing-12-month vol (point-in-time, one-month lag)
does not rescue it: net excess Sharpe **0.832** vs SPY 0.874 (advantage **−0.042**, active
NW *t* = **−1.30**). If anything it tilts harder into the low-vol/quality sleeves and lags SPY
a touch more.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful

Deterministic monthly world (market + five members each with an independent style factor +
benchmark + cash), 168 months, TUNABLE planted per-annum blend edge (`data.synthetic_world`):

| world | Sharpe adv | active (bps/mo) | active NW *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| null (edge = +0%/yr) | +0.007 | +1.5 | **+0.21** |
| planted (edge = +3%/yr) | +0.198 | +26.5 | **+3.66** |

The detector stays quiet on the null and recovers a planted blend edge cleanly. *(Machinery
proof only — never cited in support of a stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The diversification the sleeve is *sold* on is **real and mechanical**:
  the equal-weight blend carries lower vol (14.1%) and a higher excess Sharpe (0.841) than the
  *average* single factor sleeve (15.2% / 0.786), and it tames the ~7 pp/yr cross-sleeve
  dispersion. But the headline claim — *beat the market on risk-adjusted return* — is not
  supported: the excess-of-cash Sharpe advantage over SPY is **−0.033** (active NW *t* −0.73),
  the paired bootstrap CI **[−0.205, +0.077]** straddles zero (P(adv<0)=0.80), and it **flips
  sign across eras**. A genuine diversification benefit, no SPY-beating edge. Flagship-survivor
  selection is named.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs are emphatically *not* the obstacle — the sleeve turns over
  1.17% of NAV/mo (~0.3 bps/yr), so gross and net are identical to two decimals. The real,
  deliverable thing (diversification of factor-timing risk, one liquid ticket per sleeve, penny
  spreads) is trivially buyable — but what it buys is a **marginally-lower-Sharpe, lower-vol
  clone of SPY**, not a bankable market-beating edge. Real but thin → **Fragile, not
  Investable**.
